My goal when I came to Washington was to represent North Dakota. And one of the things that I heard over and over again as I was auditioning for this job or interviewing for this job, something we call a campaign, was that Dodd-Frank was really, the regulations coming out of Dodd-Frank was really crushing our small institutions. That was virtually what was supposed to prevent too big to fail now was too small to succeed. And so after receiving the assignment on the banking committee, I knew that getting regulatory relief for our small institutions, lending institutions, and keeping relationship banking alive in this country was going to be my top priority on the banking committee.

You're absolutely. And so the banking committee assignment became a top priority and then looking at and understanding the need for regulatory relief and where the best opportunity was to provide that relief. And the only thing that I can say is nothing happens here unless you work in a bipartisan way. And that was perfectly obvious. But then I also had the advantage of a great bipartisan example. in what was the Warner, Corker Bell, Corker Warner, on GSE reform, and then which later became after a series of hearings, Johnson Crapo. And so I watched that process of how support for that GSE reform, now we didn't get it done, but how support was built in a bipartisan way and said, that's how you legislate in this tunnel. I really credit Bob Corker and Mark Warner with providing such an excellent example that really led to my ability to be successful as a legislator and getting things done.

So we have this regulatory relief bill that was signed by President Trump. Talk to me a little bit about the negotiations and how that came about. I know people largely credit Chairman Crapo, yourself, John Tester, and Mark Warner and Joe Donnelly. Were there any other key players involved in sort of crafting that regulatory package?

Well, we've really started this effort in 13, kind of working across the aisle. Back then, Senator Crapel was the ranking member, but we really started having these discussions on regulatory reform. I think if you look at those the first two years it really was building the kind of relationships that we need to build to achieve a package. Then we began that work again in the what I call the Shelby years but it was obvious that Shelby had his way and that we weren't going to be able to move anything if it wasn't the Shelby bill. But yet we continued to work on it and so when When President Trump was elected, I had known Gary Cohen for a number of years as he represented here in Washington. He would come in for Goldman Sachs. We waited for negotiations between Senator Crapo and Senator Brown when those fell apart. We had a package. It's interesting because people said, boy, you pulled it together fast. And so very early on, I started talking to the largest banks saying, look, I know that there's some regulatory things that you would like to get done. But this is our top priority, which is getting regulatory relief for our small community banks and our regional banks. And I knew that it was probably a stretch to go to the regional bank area. Everybody, there was an agreement on the small institutions. There were some things like come to reform that I think some people would say there wasn't an agreement on, but I felt strongly because that increased paperwork would have such a devastating effect on lending in small organizations.
